title: Preparing pre-service physics teachers to diagnose students’ conceptions not covered by physics education textbooks
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need to prepare pre-service physics teachers to diagnose students’ conceptions that are not covered in physics education textbooks (“off-textbook” conceptions). The authors argue that although textbook-based misconceptions are commonly discussed in physics teacher education, teachers also need to recognize novel or uncommon student ideas encountered in everyday classroom practice.

To address this, the authors developed a learning environment added to an existing diagnostic competence intervention. The new unit focused on diagnosing off-textbook conceptions about the viscous behaviour of fluids. Pre-service physics teachers first completed preparatory homework comparing their own explanations of a spoon sinking in honey with scientific literature, then discussed their ideas in groups, completed a multiple-choice activation task, and practiced diagnosing authentic student statements from video vignettes in small groups. The unit was originally intended as face-to-face but was implemented online because of COVID-19.

The study was piloted twice with pre-service physics teachers at the University College of Teacher Education Styria in Austria (May 2021: N=11; December 2021: N=16). The accompanying research combined questionnaires with videotaped and transcribed group discussions to identify learning barriers and facilitating elements. The main conclusion is that participants could often spot that a student statement was incorrect, but they struggled to connect those statements to underlying conceptions and to integrate physics content knowledge with pedagogical content knowledge. The authors conclude that the learning environment likely needs stronger supports to help pre-service teachers interlink content and pedagogical reasoning when diagnosing unfamiliar student thinking.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative exploratory pilot within a design-based research approach, not an RCT or QED. The paper provides useful process evidence from videotaped sessions and questionnaires, but credibility is limited by small samples and the absence of causal testing.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper addresses an important teacher-education problem for a priority population (pre-service physics teachers), but it reports no measurable student-learning effect and no effect size. Its practical impact is suggestive rather than demonstrated, so it fits a yellow tier.

finding.finding_summary: This exploratory design-based study piloted a learning environment for pre-service physics teachers to diagnose off-textbook student conceptions about the viscous behavior of fluids (May 2021: n=11; Dec 2021: n=16). The main finding was that participants could often identify that a student statement was scientifically incorrect, but they struggled to infer the underlying conception and to connect their physics content knowledge with pedagogical content knowledge. No effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of videotaped group work, discussion/reflection transcripts, and end-of-session questionnaire responses about diagnosing student conceptions
